# Gaurav Sood

> Research, open-source software, and datasets by Gaurav Sood across statistics and research methods (calibration, prediction stability, record linkage, data collection, causal inference), name-based inference, online privacy and security, meta-science, misinformation, and the political economy of India.

- [Homepage](https://gsood.com/)
- [Data, Research, and Software](https://gsood.com/research/)
- [Goji Berries (Blog)](https://gojiberries.io/)

## Statistics and Research Methods

### Prediction Stability
- [Queue Shift: Updating Classifiers Under a Staffing Budget](https://gsood.com/research/papers/queue_shift.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/queue-shift-updating-classifiers-under-a-staffing-budget/)): When classifier predictions route cases to specialized queues, a model update changes both accuracy and the work each team receives. Queue Shift chooses the batch assignment that maximizes candidate-model probability subject to budgets on work moved between queues, counted in cases, hours, or money, and on expected negative flips. At the movement and expected flips of any comparison rule, it has at least that rule's expected accuracy under the candidate's probabilities. Simulations show that holding queue totals fixed costs little when an update mostly reorders cases and a great deal when it moves volume between queues, and that learned queue prices nearly match exact assignment in accuracy but miss the movement budget in most batches. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/queue-shift).
- [stable-cart: Lower Bootstrap Prediction Variance CART](https://github.com/finite-sample/stable-cart) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/stable-cart-lower-bootstrap-prediction-variance-cart/)): Standard CART decision trees are unstable—small changes in training data can produce substantially different tree structures and predictions. stable-cart addresses this by trading a small amount of accuracy for lower cross-bootstrap prediction variance through techniques like honest estimation (using separate data subsets for learning tree structure vs. estimating leaf values), lookahead search (considering multiple future splits before committing rather than making greedy single-step decisions), and bootstrap-aware split selection (penalizing or filtering out splits that are unstable across resampled datasets). Links: [Install package](https://pypi.org/project/stable-cart/).

### Calibration and Weighting
- [When Pooling Costs a Decision: Probability Calibration with Calibre](https://gsood.com/research/papers/calibre.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/calibration-where-it-counts-cost-and-data-informed-isotonic-regression/)): Isotonic calibration fits flat regions: runs of scores that receive one probability. A flat region costs a decision only when the cases it pools fall on both sides of the decision's threshold, and a ranking only when its ties are broken at random. Using an exact known-risk simulation and a pre-registered benchmark, the paper finds flat regions cheap for cost-threshold decisions: choosing a calibrator by validation payoff did no better than choosing it by Brier score. For allocation, random tie-breaking costs up to 1.7 successes per 1,000 cases, which breaking ties by the original score recovers exactly. Links: [calibre: Probability Calibration and Evaluation](https://github.com/finite-sample/calibre).
- [fairlex: leximin calibration](https://github.com/finite-sample/fairlex) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/fairlex-leximin-calibration/)): Standard calibration minimizes average calibration error, which can hide large errors for minority groups. Leximin calibration instead minimizes the worst-off group's calibration error first, then the second-worst, and so on—applying the Rawlsian leximin criterion to the distribution of calibration quality across groups.
- [Rank-Preserving Calibration for Multiclass Classification](https://gsood.com/research/papers/multiclass-rank-calibration.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/rank-preserving-calibration-for-multiclass-classification/)): Multiclass calibration methods can reorder predicted class probabilities, so the class a calibrated model ranks first may differ from the class the original model ranked first. This is problematic when downstream decisions depend on the ranking, not just the probabilities. We develop calibration methods that guarantee the within-example class ranking is preserved while still improving probability reliability. Links: [Rank Preserving Calibration of Multiclass Probabilities](https://github.com/finite-sample/rank-preserving-calibration).
- [Streaming Raking in Fixed Memory](https://gsood.com/research/papers/onlinerake.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/streaming-calibration-with-mwu-and-sgd/)): Raking needs every row seen so far, so keeping weights current on a stream means storing it and refitting. This paper gives a raking method whose state is a fixed set of running totals: each arriving row gets, in closed form, the weight that balances closeness to its design weight against the running gap to population targets. In simulations it comes close to full-data raking with moderate targets at constant cost per row; it falls short with extreme targets and many margins, and where rows can be stored, periodic raking remains the better choice. Links: [Python Package](https://github.com/finite-sample/onlinerake).
- [streamcal: Streaming Probability Calibration](https://github.com/finite-sample/streamcal) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/streamcal-streaming-probability-calibration/)): streamcal keeps a deployed model's binary probabilities calibrated as outcomes arrive, without retaining its prediction history. It fits a monotone (isotonic) correction from fixed-size per-bin sufficient statistics, can down-weight stale history, and predicts before observing each outcome so a forecast never uses its own label.
- [From Scores to Signs: Pairwise Win-Rate Estimation with Calibrated LLM Judges](https://gsood.com/research/papers/score_signs.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/from-scores-to-signs-pairwise-win-rate-estimation-with-calibrated-llm-judges/)): LLM-as-judge systems produce numerical scores, but downstream decisions often require pairwise comparisons: which response is better? Converting scores to win rates requires calibration—the mapping from score differences to win probabilities. We develop calibrated estimators for pairwise win rates from cardinal LLM judge scores, accounting for judge miscalibration and non-transitivity in preferences. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/score_signs).

### Record Linkage
- [setjoin: Record Linkage That Preserves Group Structure](https://github.com/finite-sample/setjoin) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/setjoin-record-linkage-that-preserves-group-structure/)): setjoin implements group-constrained record matching: it assigns source groups to target groups, then matches records within the assigned groups. This is useful when both files have trustworthy group membership and the linkage should preserve it. Its current performance example is synthetic; gains on observed panel data have not been established.
- [preclink: High-Precision Record Linkage](https://github.com/finite-sample/preclink) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/tether-high-precision-record-linkage/)): A 7-step record linkage pipeline—preprocess, deduplicate, block, score, filter, decide, inspect—with multi-pass support for progressively relaxed thresholds. Implements Hungarian, greedy, and row-sequential decision rules over pairwise string similarity scores.
- [bloomjoin: Bloom Filter Based Joins](https://github.com/gojiplus/bloomjoin) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/bloomjoin-bloom-filter-based-joins/)): An R package implementing Bloom filter-based joins for improved performance with large datasets. Bloom filters provide a probabilistic test for set membership that can dramatically reduce the number of expensive exact comparisons needed during a join.

### Data Collection
- [The Micro-Task Market for "Lemons": Collecting Data on Amazon's Mechanical Turk](https://gsood.com/research/papers/turk.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/the-micro-task-market-for-lemons-collecting-data-on-amazon-s-mechanical-turk/)): With Doug Ahler and Carrie Roush. Political Science Research and Methods, 13(1), 1–20, 2025. While Amazon's Mechanical Turk (MTurk) has reduced the cost of collecting original data, in 2018, researchers noted the potential existence of a large number of bad actors on the platform. To evaluate data quality on MTurk, we fielded three surveys between 2018 and 2020. While find no evidence of a "bot epidemic," significant portions of the data—between 25%-35%—are of dubious quality. While the number of IP addresses that completed the survey multiple times or circumvented location requirements fell almost 50% over time, suspicious IP addresses are more prevalent on MTurk than on other platforms. Furthermore, many respondents appear to respond humorously or insincerely, and this behavior increased over 200% from 2018-2020. Importantly, these low-quality responses attenuate observed treatment effects by magnitudes ranging from approximately 10-30%. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/themains/turk-replication).
- [Optimal Data Collection When Strata and Strata Variances Are Known](https://gsood.com/research/papers/optimal_data_collection.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/optimal-data-collection-when-strata-and-strata-variances-are-known/)): With Ken Cor. When the population is divided into known strata with known variances, the optimal allocation of a fixed sample budget across strata depends on stratum size, variance, and sampling cost. We derive the optimal allocation and show how much efficiency is lost by common rules of thumb like proportional allocation. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/optimal_data_collection).
- [geo-sampling: Sampling Randomly From the Streets](https://github.com/geosensing/geo-sampling) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/geo-sampling-sampling-randomly-from-the-streets/)): With Suriyan Laohaprapanon. Estimating quantities like average potholes per kilometer or pedestrian density requires randomly sampling street locations within a region. geo-sampling addresses this by downloading street network data from OpenStreetMap for a specified administrative region, splitting each street into 0.5km segments (recording the lat/long of segment endpoints), building a database of all segments, and then drawing a random sample that can be exported as a CSV or visualized on a map for field data collection. Links: [geoestimate: inference from street samples](https://github.com/geosensing/geoestimate).
- [allocator: Optimal Itineraries For Spatially Distributed Tasks](https://github.com/geosensing/allocator) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/allocator-optimal-itineraries-for-spatially-distributed-tasks/)): With Suriyan Laohaprapanon. Given a set of spatially distributed tasks (e.g., field survey locations, audit sites), allocator computes optimal itineraries that minimize total travel time or distance, assigning tasks to enumerators and sequencing visits within each assignment. Links: [ybar: mobile field data collection](https://github.com/geosensing/ybar).
- [reporoulette: Randomly Sample GitHub Repositories](https://github.com/gojiplus/reporoulette) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/reporoulette-randomly-sample-github-repositories/)): Randomly sample GitHub repositories, optionally filtered by language, creation date, or star count. Useful for constructing representative samples of open-source projects for empirical software engineering research.
- [Unbiased Regression with Costly Item Labels](https://gsood.com/research/papers/fewest-items.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/unbiased-regression-with-costly-item-labels/)): When running OLS on per-row trait shares (e.g., fraction of items in a category), labeling every item is expensive. Random labeling wastes budget on items that barely affect the regression. fewlab identifies the items with the highest statistical leverage—those that most influence the coefficient estimates—and prioritizes them for labeling, achieving unbiased OLS with a fraction of the labeling cost. Links: [fewlab: fewest items to label for unbiased OLS on shares](https://github.com/finite-sample/fewlab).
- [statqa: Extract Multimodal Stats Q/A from Tables With Provenance](https://github.com/gojiplus/statqa) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/statqa-extract-multimodal-stats-q-a-from-tables-with-provenance/)): statqa is a modern Python framework for automatically extracting structured facts, statistical insights, and multimodal Q/A pairs from tabular datasets. It converts raw columns and values into clear, human-readable statements paired with rich visualizations, enabling rapid knowledge discovery, CLIP-style multimodal RAG corpus construction, and LLM training.

### Causal Inference
- [Inferring Treatment Compliance from Delivery-Window Data](https://gsood.com/research/papers/inferred_compliance_note.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/inferring-treatment-compliance-from-delivery-window-data/)): In randomized experiments with imperfect compliance, the LATE requires observing treatment receipt, and the Wald estimator requires monotonicity. When receipt is unobserved but the experiment has a pre-treatment time series and a distinct delivery window, a structural break test applied to the delivery window can classify treated units into compliers, never-takers, and defiers. This yields an inferred compliance rate with closed-form bias correction, an empirical test of monotonicity via defier detection, and a characterization of the complier subpopulation that can be projected onto the control group. Links: [Source code](https://github.com/finite-sample/late/).
- [Regression Calibration as a Baseline for Machine-Learned Covariates](https://gsood.com/research/papers/calibration_baseline.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/two-regressions-and-a-bootstrap-regression-calibration-for-ml-generated-covariates-and-the-nonlinear-boundary/)): Researchers increasingly use machine-learning predictions as covariates, including controls for confounding. Prediction error can then change the estimated effect of interest. Regression calibration offers an established baseline: use a labeled sample to predict the true covariate from its machine-generated surrogate and the other regression variables. We explain when this procedure identifies a linear model and what can go wrong when calibration must itself be learned. A population projection can suffice without a correct conditional-mean model, but estimated calibration must preserve the residual relationships that identify the downstream coefficients. We connect departures from those relationships to coefficient error, distinguish many calibration predictors from many mismeasured covariates, and separate estimation error from failures of support and transport. Exact examples show how omitting treatment or imposing shrinkage changes confounding adjustment; simulations illustrate these mechanisms. The resulting framework makes regression calibration a transparent benchmark for evaluating methods that use machine-learned covariates. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/calibration-baseline).
- [Which Prediction Errors Matter? Finite Covariate-Correction Paths for Downstream Regression](https://gsood.com/research/papers/validation_swaps.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/partial-credit-diagnosing-proxy-covariates-with-validation-swaps/)): Correcting errors in machine-learned covariates can change a treatment-effect estimate in ways that separate corrections do not predict. Each correction changes the regression's adjustment for other variables, so its effect can depend on which errors have already been corrected. Existing methods use verified measurements to correct inference and guide validation. We study the joint effects of finite corrections on a fitted coefficient. Our diagnostic replaces sets of proxy covariates with verified values and compares the resulting refits with the sum of isolated correction effects. Exact least-squares identities locate the source of nonadditivity in changes to the regression's cross-product matrix. Correction paths describe how the coefficient moves as more measurements are corrected, and their dispersion describes how much the choice of correction set matters. Established Shapley methods attribute the endpoint change. Simulations illustrate these distinctions. Applications to housing and text-coded incivility compare refits with three additive approximations: isolated corrections track small random correction sets closely but misstate the full correction. The resulting diagnostic measures both the consequences of individual errors and the additional changes produced by correcting them together. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/swaps).
- [One Label, Many Records: Shared Prediction Error in Regression](https://gsood.com/research/papers/total_error.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/total-error/)): One predicted item label can enter many records and several constructed variables. This paper traces the consequences for coefficients and standard errors when aggregates are regression outcomes, covariates, or both. It connects generated-variable and shared-source inference, gives joint moment corrections and covariance estimates under item validation, and states the additional conditions required for normal coefficient intervals. Simulations distinguish coefficient bias, empirical variability, estimated standard errors, and coverage, including failures with influential or few items. Browsing-data illustrations show the roles of reuse, visit concentration, and observed classifier disagreement. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/total_error).
- [Smooth Operator: Optimal Filtering of Event Study Estimates](https://gsood.com/research/papers/smooth_operator.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/smooth-operator-optimal-filtering-of-event-study-estimates/)): Event study designs estimate period-specific treatment effects with known standard errors from two-way fixed effects regressions. We treat the coefficient sequence as observations from a local linear trend state-space model and apply the Rauch–Tung–Striebel (Kalman) smoother, using the known heteroskedastic regression standard errors as observation noise. The smoother adapts to local precision—trusting the trend model when a period's estimate is noisy and trusting the data when it is tight—reducing level MSE by 80% and derivative MSE by 98% versus raw estimates, while also providing a derivative-based parallel trends test with correct size. Links: [Source code](https://github.com/finite-sample/smooth-operator).
- [Causal Debiasing for Robust Machine Learning](https://gsood.com/research/papers/causalml.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/causal-debiasing-for-robust-machine-learning/)): Spurious associations in training data arise because models learn correlations rather than causal relations. We propose a composite loss that incorporates causal and behavioral priors: an invariance penalty for label-preserving perturbations (e.g., swapping gendered pronouns should not change predictions), a directional penalty for perturbations that should change the label in a known direction, and a falsification penalty inspired by epidemiological negative controls that discourages reliance on features with no causal relationship to the outcome. The framework unifies ideas from CheckList-style behavioral testing, causal inference, and adversarial robustness into a single training objective.
- [Randomized Assignment-Based Anticlustering for Experiments with Many Arms](https://gsood.com/research/papers/randaba.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/randomized-assignment-based-anticlustering-for-experiments-with-many-arms/)): Assignment-based anticlustering splits units into equal groups that are as alike as possible and scales to millions of units, but it is deterministic. Jittering the sort that defines its batches and shuffling the group labels make it an experimental design with exact randomization inference. Each of its steps turns out to be the greedy allocation of the multi-arm adaptive design ARMM, found by an assignment problem instead of a search over all orderings of the arms. In simulations with 4 to 50 arms, it balanced covariate means better than every other design whose cost is linear in the number of units, by a margin that grew with the number of arms; run on the covariates and their squares, it gave the smallest error and the most power for a nonlinear outcome in nearly every setting.

### Other
- [One Concept at a Time: Subspace-Constrained Causal Inference for High-Dimensional Treatments](https://gsood.com/research/papers/steer.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/one-concept-at-a-time-subspace-constrained-causal-inference-for-high-dimensional-treatments/)): Social scientists increasingly wish to reason causally about high-dimensional treatments (texts, images, prompts) while isolating the effect of a single latent concept. We treat a pretrained model as a measurement device and use minimal edit pairs to estimate a concept-tangent subspace in activation space, with diagnostics that can explicitly reject the existence of a clean subspace for a given encoder and concept. When diagnostics are favorable, activation-steering maps constrained to the subspace generate approximate minimal edits, and concept coordinates serve as treatments in a double/debiased ML estimator. The resulting estimand is a local, representation-dependent linear effect—not a universal causal effect of the underlying human concept.
- [incline: Estimate Trend at a Particular Point in Time in a Noisy Time Series](https://github.com/finite-sample/incline) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/incline-estimate-trend-at-a-particular-point-in-time-in-a-noisy-time-series/)): Estimating the trend (derivative) at a specific point in a noisy time series is difficult because naive approaches like computing differences between consecutive observations amplify noise rather than reveal the underlying signal. incline addresses this by first smoothing the time series using either Savitzky-Golay filters (local polynomial fitting) or smoothing splines, then estimating the first or second derivative of the smoothed function at chosen points in time. The difference between naive and smoothed estimates can be substantial: in the provided example, the correlation between them is -0.47, making the choice of method consequential for applications like detecting sudden cost increases or identifying rapidly changing patient health trajectories.
- [hbw: Bandwidth Selection for Kernel Density Estimation and Regression](https://github.com/finite-sample/hbw) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/analytic-hessian-bandwidth-selection/)): hbw selects smoothing bandwidths by cross-validation for kernel density estimation and Nadaraya–Watson regression. It extends hessband to multivariate data. Links: [hessband (archived predecessor)](https://github.com/finite-sample/hessband).
- [A Lightweight ALS Solver for Iterative GLS](https://github.com/finite-sample/alsgls) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/a-lightweight-als-solver-for-iterative-gls/)): Generalized least squares requires estimating and inverting the error covariance matrix, which is expensive when the matrix is large or unstructured. This package uses alternating least squares with a low-rank factor-analytic decomposition of the covariance, making iterative GLS feasible for problems where the full covariance is too large to invert directly.
- [Optimal Classification Cutoffs for F1-score, etc.](https://github.com/finite-sample/optimal-classification-cutoffs) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/optimal-classification-cutoffs-for-f1-score-etc/)): Classifiers produce continuous scores; deployment requires a threshold. The optimal threshold depends on the metric you care about—F1, balanced accuracy, or a custom cost function—and the score distribution. This script computes the exact threshold that maximizes a given stepwise metric, avoiding the grid-search approximation common in practice. Links: [Install package](https://pypi.org/project/optimal-classification-cutoffs/).
- [pyppur: Projection Pursuit Dimension Reduction With Reconstruction Loss](https://github.com/finite-sample/pyppur) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/pyppur-projection-pursuit-dimension-reduction-with-reconstruction-loss/)): pyppur is a Python package that implements projection pursuit methods for dimensionality reduction. Unlike traditional PP objectives geared toward finding 'interesting' projections (non-gaussian), pyppur focuses on finding non-linear projections by minimizing either reconstruction loss or distance distortion.
- [Scaling ML Products At Startups: A Practitioner's Guide](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.10660) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/scaling-ml-products-at-startups-a-practitioner-s-guide/)): With Atul Dhingra. arXiv:2304.10660, 2023. How should a machine learning startup serve more queries, faster and of more kinds, without costs running away? We split costs into variable costs, of serving models and keeping them performant, and fixed costs, of developing and training new ones, and suggest ways to cut each. Since the largest fixed cost is often finding the root causes of failures, we also describe how we approach that.

## Names and Name-Based Inference
- [Predicting Race and Ethnicity From the Sequence of Characters in a Name](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.02109) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/predicting-race-and-ethnicity-from-sequence-of-characters-in-a-name/)): With Rajashekar Chintalapati and Suriyan Laohaprapanon. arXiv:1805.02109, first posted in 2018 and revised in 2023. The authors compare models that use the letters in a name to estimate recorded race and ethnicity. Their best model classifies 85% of held-out cases correctly using full names. With surnames alone, the best model classifies 81% correctly. Links: [ethnicolr Python package](https://github.com/appeler/ethnicolr), [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2019/04/gaurav-sood-predict-race), [AnacondaCON presentation (Video)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fuHAPENWVIU).
- [Sound Names: Classify Names Based on Sequence of Sounds](https://github.com/appeler/sound_names) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/sound-names-classify-names-based-on-sequence-of-sounds/)): We compare name classification using phonetic encodings with classification using character sequences. In the reported experiments, an LSTM trained on Metaphone encodings performs worse, suggesting that spellings contain information lost by the sound encoding.
- [Graphic Names: Classify Names Using Google Image Search and Clarifai](https://github.com/appeler/graphic_names) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/graphic-names-classify-names-using-google-image-search-and-clarifai/)): An exploratory method that combines image-search results for first names with image tags to estimate gender associations. Validation uses labeled name data, while the project notes that search results are not representative population samples and names need not be unique to one gender.
- [naampy: Infer Sociodemographic Characteristics from Indian Names](https://github.com/appeler/naampy) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/naampy-infer-sociodemographic-characteristics-from-indian-names/)): With Rajashekar Chintalapati and Suriyan Laohaprapanon. naampy estimates aggregate patterns associated with Indian first names using calibrated model scores or exact source-data lookups. Results include abstention and artifact provenance; the scores describe patterns in recorded labels, not an individual's gender. Links: [outkast: caste-name data](https://github.com/appeler/outkast), [Indian electoral rolls](https://github.com/in-rolls/electoral_rolls).
- [pranaam: Predict Religion From Name](https://github.com/appeler/pranaam) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/pranaam-predict-religion-from-name/)): With Rajashekar Chintalapati. pranaam estimates how strongly a name follows patterns associated with Muslim names in its training data. It returns a calibrated score, abstention information, and artifact provenance for aggregate research, rather than establishing a person's religion.
- [naamkaran: a generative model for names](https://github.com/appeler/naamkaran) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/naamkaran-a-generative-model-for-names/)): With Rajashekar Chintalapati. A character-level LSTM trained on Florida voter-registration names generates synthetic name-like strings. The outputs are intended for demonstrations, testing, and exploration, rather than verified names or representative samples of a population.
- [parsernaam: ML-assisted name parser](https://github.com/appeler/parsernaam) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/parsernaam-ml-assisted-name-parser/)): With Rajashekar Chintalapati. parsernaam uses character-level models to distinguish first-name from last-name tokens and infer their order in multi-token strings. It helps parse combined name fields, while its limited label set cannot represent every naming convention. Links: [clean-names: parsing and deduplication](https://github.com/appeler/clean-names).
- [instate: State and Language Composition from Indian Surnames](https://github.com/appeler/instate) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/instate-predict-spoken-language-from-last-name/)): With Rajashekar Chintalapati and Atul Dhingra. instate estimates state composition associated with Indian surnames using electoral-roll lookups and a calibrated character model. It combines state shares with census mother-tongue shares to derive aggregate language compositions; these are name-pattern estimates, not a person's location or language. Links: [Instate: Predict the State of Residence from Last Name.](https://gsood.com/research/papers/instate.pdf).

## Online Privacy and Security
- [Exposed: Shedding Blacklight On Online Privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24041) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/exposed-shedding-blacklight-on-online-privacy/)): With Lucas Shen. To what extent are users surveilled on the web, by what technologies, and by whom? We answer these questions by combining passively observed, anonymized browsing data of a large, representative sample of Americans with domain-level data on tracking from Blacklight. We find that nearly all users (>99%) encounter at least one ad tracker or third-party cookie over the observation window. More invasive techniques like session recording, keylogging, and canvas fingerprinting are less widespread, but over half of the users visited a site employing at least one of these within the first 48 hours of the start of tracking. Linking trackers to their parent organizations reveals that a single organization, usually Google, can track over 50% of web activity of more than half the users. Demographic differences in exposure are modest and often attenuate when we account for browsing volume. However, disparities by age and race remain, suggesting that what users browse, not just how much, shapes their surveillance risk. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/themains/private_blacklight/).
- [Pwned: The Risk of Exposure From Data Breaches](https://gsood.com/research/papers/pwned.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/pwned-how-often-are-americans-online-accounts-breached/)): With Ken Cor. ACM Web Science Conference, 289–293, 2019. We looked up one email address for each of 5,000 U.S. adults in the July 2018 Have I Been Pwned database. At least one record appeared for 82.84% of the sample. After excluding spam lists, 71.78% still had a recorded exposure. Both figures describe the email address we queried for each person. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/themains/pwned_survey/), [Bob Rudis Analyzes Exposure by Breach](https://rud.is/b/2018/07/29/ggplot-doodling-with-hibp-breaches/), [I Have Been Pwned: Evidence from the Florida Voter Registration Data](https://github.com/themains/pwned_voters), [Supporting Information](https://gsood.com/research/papers/pwned_si.pdf), [Exposure counts and denominators](https://github.com/themains/pwned_survey/blob/master/results/totals.csv).
- [piedomains: Predict the Kind of Content Hosted by a Domain](https://github.com/themains/piedomains) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/piedomains-predict-the-kind-of-content-hosted-by-a-domain/)): With Rajashekar Chintalapati. The package infers the kind of content hosted by a domain using the domain name, the textual content, and the screenshot of the homepage. We use domain category labels from Shallalist and build our own training dataset by scraping and taking screenshots of the homepage. Links: [Domain Knowledge: Predicting the Kind of Content Hosted by a Domain.](https://gsood.com/research/papers/domain_knowledge.pdf), [rdomains: domain classification in R](https://github.com/themains/rdomains), [13th International Conference on Computational Intelligence in Security for Information Systems (CISIS 2020), pp. 152–162.](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-57805-3_15).
- [Pass-Fail: Using a Password Generator to Improve Password Strength](https://github.com/themains/password) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/pass-fail-using-a-password-generator-to-improve-password-strength/)): With Rajashekar Chintalapati. We train character-level models on leaked passwords to study predictable password choices. Comparisons with Have I Been Pwned and randomly generated strings show how learned patterns, including common starting characters, can help diagnose password weakness.
- [How Often is Politicians' Data Breached? Evidence from HIBP](https://gsood.com/research/papers/pwned_politicians.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/how-often-is-politicians-data-breached-evidence-from-hibp/)): With Lucas Shen. Using 12,384 email addresses of politicians from 59 countries, we examine exposure to breaches recorded by Have I Been Pwned. A third of the politicians have at least one recorded breach, and more than one in five have sensitive information exposed; incomplete coverage of their email addresses makes these conservative estimates. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/themains/pwned_pols).
- [Bad Domains: Exposure to Malicious Content Online](https://gsood.com/research/papers/bad_domains.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/bad-domains-exposure-to-malicious-content-online/)): With Lucas Shen. Information, Communication & Society, 2026. We combine a month of observed browsing by over a thousand Americans with malicious-domain classifications. About half visited a malicious domain; demographic differences in median exposure disappear after accounting for how much people use the internet. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/themains/bad_domains/).
- [Social Proof is in the Pudding: The (Non)-Impact of Social Proof on Software Downloads](https://gsood.com/research/papers/social_proof_stars.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/social-proof-is-in-the-pudding-the-non-impact-of-social-proof-on-software-downloads/)): With Lucas Shen and Daniel Weitzel. Journal of Online Trust and Safety, 3(2), 2026. Open-source software is widely used in commercial applications. Pair that with the fact that when choosing open-source software for a new problem, developers often use social proof as a cue. These two facts raise concern that bad actors can game social proof metrics to induce the use of malign software. We study the question using two field experiments. On the largest developer platform, GitHub, we buy ‘stars’ for a random set of GitHub repositories of new Python packages and estimate their impact on package downloads. We find no discernible impact. In another field experiment, we manipulate the number of human downloads for Python packages. Again, we find little effect. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/themains/social_proof_stars/).
- [Know Your IP](https://github.com/themains/know-your-ip/) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/know-your-ip/)): With Suriyan Laohaprapanon. A Python toolkit for enriching IP addresses with registration, network, geolocation, and reputation information from multiple providers. It reconciles provider outputs while recording provenance, caching results, and handling rate limits and partial failures.
- [virustotal: R Client for the VirusTotal API v3](https://github.com/themains/virustotal) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/virustotal-r-client-for-the-virustotal-public-api-2-0/)): An R client for VirusTotal API v3, covering reports on files, URLs, domains, and IP addresses, as well as submissions for analysis. The package includes request pacing, retries, and structured error handling.

## Software and Tools
- [rmcp: R MCP Community Server](https://github.com/finite-sample/rmcp) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/rmcp-r-mcp-community-server/)): A Model Context Protocol server that lets compatible assistants invoke R tools for statistical analysis. Its documented tools cover regression, econometrics, time series, statistical testing, and data exploration.
- [🍠 tuber: Access YouTube API via R](https://github.com/gojiplus/tuber) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/tuber-access-youtube-api-via-r/)): An R client for searching and retrieving YouTube videos, channels, playlists, comments, and captions. It also supports selected authenticated operations, including uploads, moderation, and playlist updates. Links: [tubern: YouTube Analytics and Reporting](https://github.com/gojiplus/tubern).
- [repaper: convert photo of a form to a web based form or an editable pdf form](https://github.com/pvbhanuteja/repaper) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/repaper-convert-photo-of-a-form-to-a-web-based-form-or-an-editable-pdf-form/)): With Bhanu Teja. repaper converts photographed forms into editable digital forms. The documented workflow includes generating a Google Form from an image through a Python interface or command-line tool. Links: [image-to-text: batch OCR](https://github.com/gojiplus/image-to-text).
- [indicate: Transliterate Indic Languages to English](https://github.com/in-rolls/indicate) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/indicate-transliterate-indic-languages-to-english/)): With Rajashekar Chintalapati. A transliteration toolkit for converting between Indic scripts and English-script representations. It supports composable word-table, local-model, and language-model backends, with batch processing and structured output.
- [Lost Years: Expected Number of Years Lost](https://github.com/gojiplus/lost-years) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/lost-years-expected-number-of-years-lost/)): With Suriyan Laohaprapanon. Mortality rate is puzzling to mortals. A better number is the expected number of years lost. (A yet better number would be quality-adjusted years lost.) To make it easier to calculate the expected years lost, lost_years provides a convenient way to join to the SSA actuarial data, HLD data, and WHO life table data.
- [Weather Data by Location and Date](https://github.com/gojiplus/get-weather-data) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/get-weather-data/)): A Python package and web interface for retrieving historical daily weather by US ZIP code or coordinates. It uses NOAA station data, selects nearby stations, and returns weather measures in metric or imperial units.
- [layoutlens: AI-Assisted UI Testing](https://github.com/gojiplus/layoutlens) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/layoutlens-ai-assisted-ui-testing/)): layoutlens captures screenshots, page structure, styles, and geometry to measure changes between interface versions. Local comparisons report element-level differences and possible layout defects; model-based explanations are optional. Links: [layoutlens GitHub Action](https://github.com/gojiplus/layoutlens-action), [UI Judge Benchmark](https://github.com/gojiplus/uijudge-bench).
- [preen: Python Package Development Checks](https://github.com/gojiplus/preen) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/preen-python-package-development/)): preen helps Python packages adopt and maintain the py-canon development standard. Its command-line tools scaffold repositories, update shared templates, check conformance, apply fixes, and guide tag-based releases. Links: [py-canon: shared Python package standards](https://github.com/gojiplus/py-canon), [r-canon: shared R package standards](https://github.com/gojiplus/r-canon).
- [Offprint: A Jekyll Theme for Academic Websites](https://github.com/gojiplus/jekyll-theme-offprint) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/offprint-academic-website-theme/)): A Jekyll theme for academic personal websites, with a single text column and publications rendered from structured data. It uses self-hosted fonts and system-controlled dark mode, without requiring JavaScript.
- [adjacent — Related Repositories Recommender](https://github.com/gojiplus/adjacent/) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/adjacent-related-repositories-recommender/)): A GitHub Action that adds related-repository recommendations to a README. It ranks repositories using shared topics, README similarity, or a combination, with controls for exclusions and the number of recommendations. Links: [Use GitHub Action](https://github.com/gojiplus/adjacent#setup).
- [Advertiser: Promote Your GitHub Repositories on Bluesky](https://github.com/gojiplus/advertiser) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/advertiser-promote-your-github-repositories-on-bluesky/)): A GitHub Action that selects a repository from a curated list, generates a short description, and posts it with a link to Bluesky. It supports automated or manually triggered promotion of open-source projects. Links: [Use GitHub Action](https://github.com/gojiplus/advertiser#use-in-another-repository).

## Meta Science

### Software Use and Credit
- [Downloads Are Cheap: Validated Use as a Measure of Research Software](https://gsood.com/research/papers/downloads_are_cheap.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/downloads-are-cheap-validated-use-as-a-measure-of-research-software/)): Counts of research software use allocate credit, and the available ones are cheap to produce: a download is one fetch of a file. I propose validated use, a package loaded in replication code deposited at a journal that checks it, as a costly signal, and measure it in 13,245 deposits from 75 economics and political science journal collections, which load 4,565 R, Python and Stata packages. Among packages the corpus uses, validated use and downloads agree loosely, and least where automatic installation is commonest: the rank correlation is 0.61 for Stata, 0.53 for R and 0.36 for Python. Downloads track a package's position in the dependency graph more closely than its use. The most used software prepares exhibits: estout is in 43% of Stata deposits. Stata appears in 1.4 times as many deposits as R and is missing from studies of research software because its packages are scattered across SSC, two journals' archives and authors' sites with no index across them. I build that index, 10,147 commands in 5,581 packages, and release it with the mention-level data. Links: [Code](https://github.com/recite/softverse), [Data](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21943908), [Stata command index](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21926099), [Look up a package](https://recite.github.io/softverse/lookup/), [Recode: citation reminders](https://github.com/recite/recode), [pip-fund: funding software](https://github.com/recite/pip-fund).
- [user: Estimate Python Package Use on GitHub](https://github.com/recite/user) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/user-auto-compute-citations-to-software-from-github/)): This project estimates Python package use by sampling public GitHub repositories and counting import statements. It provides data and a dashboard as an alternative to download counts, which can reflect automated installation rather than adoption. Links: [Python metrics](https://github.com/recite/countpy).

### Miscitations
- [Methodological Criticism and Continued Citation](https://gsood.com/research/papers/niewenhuis.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/significant-error-citations-to-research-with-publicized-statistical-errors/)): With Ken Cor. Finding an error can improve later research only if researchers respond to it. We examine citations after methodological audits in neuroscience, animal experiments, and political science. OpenAlex histories through 2025 show continued citation to flagged neuroscience papers: their median annual citations rose from 6.5 in 2010 to 14–19 during 2012–2015 and were 7 in 2025. Comparisons within the same journal and publication year suggest somewhat slower proportional citation growth after the critique. A separate sample of citing passages rarely acknowledged a concern. The paper distinguishes persistent attention from the effect of publicity on citation growth. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/recite/sig_fault/).
- [Propagation of Error: Citations to Retracted Research](https://gsood.com/research/papers/error.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/propagation-of-error-approving-citations-to-problematic-research/)): With Ken Cor. We compare each of 8,627 retracted research articles, published 2000–2019 and retracted 2005–2022, with up to five articles from the same journal and publication year matched on pre-retraction citations, using OpenAlex citation histories through 2025 for both. In the three complete years after the retraction year, citations to retracted articles were 62% lower than the path of their comparison articles implies, and the gap keeps widening for a decade. Retracted articles nonetheless continue to be cited: across 8,963 retracted articles, 27% of all citations arrived after the retraction year, five years on 39% of the articles observed that long were still being cited, and in a hand-coded sample 91% of post-retraction citations noted no concern with the cited article. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/recite/propagation_of_error/).
- [Get Notified When Cited Article is Retracted](https://github.com/recite/retract) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/get-notified-when-cited-article-is-retracted/)): A GitHub Action that checks BibTeX references against Retraction Watch data and opens an issue when it finds a potentially retracted citation. It matches by DOI or bibliographic information and can run on a schedule or after bibliography changes. Links: [Use GitHub Action](https://github.com/recite/retract#github-action), [Highlight Citations to Retracted Articles (archived web app)](https://github.com/recite/re-cite.org).
- [AutoSum: Summarize Publications Automatically and Discover Miscitations](https://github.com/recite/autosum) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/autosum-summarize-publications-automatically-and-discover-miscitations/)): AutoSum collects passages surrounding citations to a publication in openly accessible papers. Collating these passages provides a view of how other scholars summarize the work and helps identify possible miscitations.

### Other
- [A Benchmark For Benchmarks](https://gsood.com/research/papers/benchmark.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/a-benchmark-for-benchmarks/)): This note proposes a framework for constructing interpretable machine-learning benchmarks. It emphasizes defining the task and target population before choosing data, and assessing label quality and whether performance reflects the intended capability.
- [Review of "Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment"](https://gsood.com/research/papers/noise_review.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/review-of-noise-a-flaw-in-human-judgment/)): With Andrew Gelman. CHANCE, 37(3), 70–72, 2024. A review of Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment that examines variation in judgments made from the same information. We consider what disagreement reveals about uncertainty, skill, effort, preferences, and the institutions in which decisions are made.
- [By the Numbers: Toward More Precise Numerical Summaries of Results](https://gsood.com/research/papers/quant.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/by-the-numbers-toward-more-precise-numerical-summaries-of-results/)): With Andrew Guess. The Political Methodologist. 24(1): 2016. We compare how often empirical articles in the American Political Science Review and American Economic Review include precise numerical results in their abstracts. The project provides coded data and analysis of differences in quantitative reporting. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/recite/quant-discipline).
- [The Review: Production and Consumption of APSR Articles](https://github.com/recite/meta_ps) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/the-review-production-and-consumption-of-apsr-articles/)): We collect article metadata from five political science journals to examine changes in authorship, article length, and readership. The data document the rise of coauthorship and the highly uneven distribution of article and abstract views.
- [studyframe: Persistent Metadata for R Data Frames](https://github.com/gojiplus/superdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/superdf-save-metadata-with-the-data-in-r-and-python-dataframes/)): studyframe extends R data frames with metadata such as version, author, and notes. The metadata is designed to persist through common data operations and input/output, keeping documentation attached to the data.
- [Not to Code: Evidence From Static Code Analysis of Replication Scripts](https://github.com/recite/not_to_code) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/not-to-code-evidence-from-static-code-analysis-of-replication-scripts/)): We apply static analysis to R scripts in replication archives for American Journal of Political Science articles. The project documents style issues, warnings, and errors detected by lintr and provides the scripts used for the audit.

## Public Services and Infrastructure
- [Predicting Out of Home Placement](https://gsood.com/research/papers/ooh_pred.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/predicting-out-of-home-placement/)): Can administrative and clinical records help target limited assessment capacity toward youth likely to enter behavioral health out-of-home care? We study 15,332 New Jersey youth with pre-2015 CANS assessments in a PerformCare cohort selected through service involvement during 2014–2015. We use assessments, demographics, diagnoses, medications, and eligibility records dated before January 1, 2015 to predict recorded admission starts through November 2, 2016. Among 3,067 held-out youth, selecting the 100 highest model scores identifies 28 youth with a recorded placement, compared with 23 using prior placement history and 5.9 expected under random selection. The incremental gain over the history rule at this capacity is uncertain. These are gains in case finding, not estimates of placements prevented or welfare improved. Retrospective cohort selection and uncertain admission completeness limit prospective interpretation. Links: [Code](https://github.com/soodoku/ooh_pred).
- [StreetSense: Learning from Google Street View](https://gsood.com/research/papers/street_sense.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/streetsense-learning-from-google-street-view/)): With Suriyan Laohaprapanon and Kimberly Ortleb. How good are the public services and the public infrastructure? Does their quality vary by income? These are vital questions—they shed light on how well the government is doing its job, the consequences of disparities in local funding, etc. But there is little good data on many of these questions. We fill this gap by describing a scalable method of getting data on one crucial piece of public infrastructure: roads. We assess the quality of roads and sidewalks by exploiting data from Google Street View. We randomly sample locations on major roads, query Google Street View images for those locations and code the images using Amazon’s Mechanical Turk. We apply this method to assess the quality of roads in Bangkok, Jakarta, Lagos, and Wayne County, Michigan. Jakarta’s roads have nearly four times the potholes than roads of any other city. Surprisingly, the proportion of road segments with potholes in Bangkok, Lagos, and Wayne is about the same, between .06 and .07. Using the data, we also estimate the relation between the condition of the roads and local income in Wayne, MI. We find that roads in more affluent census tracts have somewhat fewer potholes. Links: [arXiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.06075.pdf), [Replication Materials](https://github.com/geosensing/streetsense).
- [AutoSense: Automated Street Condition Assessment](https://github.com/geosensing/autosense) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/autosense-automated-street-condition-assessment/)): AutoSense combines sampled street locations from OpenStreetMap with street-level imagery and computer vision for assessing street conditions. The workflow supports collection and analysis of infrastructure imagery at scale.
- [Get in Line: Waiting Times at the DMV](https://github.com/soodoku/wait) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/get-in-line-waiting-times-at-the-dmv/)): With Noah Finberg. We collect reported waiting times for California DMV field offices to study variation by location, day, and hour. The analysis also examines relationships between waiting times and local sociodemographic characteristics.
- [Public Sector Salaries: Data on US Public Employees](https://github.com/soodoku/public_salaries_data) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/public-sector-salaries/)): A collection of public-employee salary data and supporting acquisition tools. The project aims to compare compensation across places and over time, with contextual information for analyses of local public spending and pay.

## Knowledge and Misinformation
- [You Cannot be Serious: The Impact of Accuracy Incentives on Partisan Bias](https://gsood.com/research/papers/PartisanBias.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/you-cannot-be-serious-the-impact-of-accuracy-incentives-on-partisan-bias/)): With Markus Prior and Kabir Khanna. Quarterly Journal of Political Science. 10(4), 489–518, 2015. Two national survey experiments test whether partisan gaps in reports of economic conditions reflect differences in knowledge or how people answer. Monetary incentives and appeals for accuracy reduce the gaps, suggesting that ordinary survey responses mix factual beliefs with partisan expression. Links: [Online Appendix](https://gsood.com/research/papers/PartisanCheerleadingAppendix.pdf), [Washington Monthly](https://gsood.com/research/press/PartisanBiasWashingtonMonthly.pdf), [Pacific Standard](https://gsood.com/research/press/PartisanBiasPacificStandard.pdf), [The New York Times](https://gsood.com/research/press/PartisanBiasNYT.pdf), [Partisan Gaps in Retrospection are Highly Variable](https://gsood.com/research/papers/partisanRetrospection.pdf), [Blog Post](http://gojiberries.io/the-value-of-money-learning-from-experiments-offering-money-for-correct-answers/).
- [Motivated Responding in Studies of Factual Learning](https://gsood.com/research/papers/partisanlearning.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/motivated-responding-in-studies-of-factual-learning/)): With Kabir Khanna. Political Behavior. 40(1): 79–101, 2018. Three experiments use accuracy incentives to distinguish biased learning from biased reporting of learned information. Incentives increase accurate reporting of politically uncongenial results, but also increase skepticism about their credibility, suggesting that bias can shift from one judgment to another. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/know_motivated), [Blog Summarizing the Paper](https://politicalbehavior.wordpress.com/2017/03/02/motivated-responding-in-studies-of-factual-learning/), [The Innumerate American](http://gojiberries.io/the-innumerate-american/).
- [A Gap in Our Understanding? Reconsidering the Evidence for Partisan Knowledge Gaps](https://gsood.com/research/papers/partisan_gap.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/a-gap-in-our-understanding-reconsidering-the-evidence-for-partisan-knowledge-gaps/)): With Carrie Roush. Quarterly Journal of Political Science, 18(1), 131–151, 2023. Across 162,083 responses to 187 questions on 47 surveys, partisan knowledge gaps are smaller and less consistently aligned with partisan interests than often assumed. Vague response options inflate some gaps, suggesting a role for motivated responding rather than differences in stored knowledge alone. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/know_pgap_review), [An Unclear Gap: Partisan Cues and Evaluations of the Same Economic Information](https://gsood.com/research/papers/unclear_gap.pdf), [Not Another Politics Podcast (U. Chicago)](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/do-partisans-really-believe-different-facts/id1496412542?i=1000623917602).
- [The Waters of Casablanca: On Political Misinformation](https://gsood.com/research/papers/CasablancaTheory.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/the-waters-of-casablanca-on-political-misinformation/)): With Robert C. Luskin. Misinformation is a confidently held false belief, distinct from knowledge, mere belief, and ignorance. Multiple-choice items cannot tell it from guessing; asking how definitely true or false each statement is can. In four surveys that randomly assigned the two formats, the scale finds far less misinformation about well-publicized falsehoods, and much smaller partisan gaps, than multiple-choice items do. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/know_casablanca).
- [Mis-measuring Political Knowledge? Do People Know More—or Even Less—about Politics than Commonly Thought?](https://gsood.com/research/papers/HiddenKnowledge.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/mis-measuring-political-knowledge/)): With Robert C. Luskin and Daniel Weitzel. Revisionist studies argue that surveys understate political knowledge. Randomized experiments in three online surveys, and a recount of ANES and NAES items and don't-know probes, find little hidden knowledge: photos lower correct identification of officials, menus and probes add little beyond guessing, and asking how sure people are finds far less knowledge than multiple choice. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/know_hidden).
- [Misinformation About Misinformation? Of Headlines and Survey Design](https://gsood.com/research/papers/misinformation_misinformation.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/misinformation-about-misinformation-of-headlines-and-survey-design/)): With Robert C. Luskin, Yul Min Park, and Joshua Blank. Media-poll misinformation items rarely offer a 'don't know' and usually ask what respondents think. In a survey experiment, offering and encouraging 'don't know' cut incorrect answers from 32% to 20%, repeating the false claim in the question changed nothing, and asking how definitely true or false each statement is cut them to 7%. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/know_misinfo_misinfo).
- [Misinformed About the Affordable Care Act? Leveraging Certainty to Assess the Prevalence of Misinformation](https://gsood.com/research/papers/ACAMisinformed.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/misinformed-about-the-affordable-care-act-leveraging-certainty-to-assess-the-prevalence-of-misinformation/)): With Josh Pasek and Jon Krosnick. Journal of Communication. 65(4): 660–673, 2015. Two national surveys distinguish incorrect answers about the Affordable Care Act from confidently held incorrect beliefs. Most respondents are uncertain; confident misperceptions are less common and are concentrated on provisions about which elites repeatedly made false claims. Links: [Supporting Information](https://gsood.com/research/papers/ACAMisinformedSI.pdf), [Replication Materials](https://osf.io/ya7wd/).
- [Guessing and Forgetting: A Latent Class Model for Measuring Learning](https://gsood.com/research/papers/guess.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/guessing-and-forgetting-a-latent-class-model-for-measuring-learning/)): With Ken Cor. Political Analysis. 24(2): 226–242, 2016. We develop a latent class model to estimate learning when correct answers can result from guessing. Under an assumption of no knowledge loss over short periods, simulations recover learning more accurately than raw score differences; an application to Deliberative Polls raises learning estimates and reduces measured gender gaps. Links: [Ed Haertel](http://web.stanford.edu/~haertel/), [R Package](https://github.com/finite-sample/guess), [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/know_guess_forget).
- [Measuring Learning in Informative Processes](https://gsood.com/research/papers/k_gains.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/measuring-learning-in-informative-processes/)): With Robert Luskin and Ariel Helfer. Observed knowledge gain can understate learning when those who know more also learn more and easy questions limit their room to improve. The paper derives conditions under which post-process knowledge is more closely associated with true learning. It performs better in proportional-learning simulations matched to 21 Deliberative Polls, but observed gain does better in catch-up simulations and most split-item comparisons. Scoring and baseline adjustment also change associations with education and attitude change. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/know_gains).
- [A Measurement Gap? Effect of the Survey Instrument and Scoring on the Partisan Knowledge Gap](https://gsood.com/research/papers/measurement_gap.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/a-measurement-gap-effect-of-the-survey-instrument-and-scoring-on-the-partisan-knowledge-gap/)): With Lucas Shen and Daniel Weitzel. Public Opinion Quarterly, 89(3), 812–836, 2025. Research suggests that partisan gaps in political knowledge with partisan implications are wide and widespread. Using a series of experiments, we investigate the extent to which partisan gaps in commercial surveys are a result of differences in beliefs than motivated guessing. Knowledge items on commercial surveys often have features that encourage guessing. We find that removing such features yields scales with greater reli- ability and higher criterion validity. More substantively, partisan gaps on scales without these “inflationary” features are roughly 40% smaller. Thus, contrary to Prior, Sood and Khanna (2015), who find that the upward bias is explained by the knowledgeable deliberately marking the wrong answer (partisan cheerleading), our data suggest, in line with Bullock et al. (2015) and Graham and Yair (2023), that partisan gaps on commercial surveys are strongly upwardly biased by motivated guessing by the ignorant. Relatedly, we also find that partisans know less than what toplines of commercial polls suggest. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/know_pgap_format).
- [An Unclear Gap: Partisan Cues and Evaluations of the Same Economic Information](https://gsood.com/research/papers/unclear_gap.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/an-unclear-gap-how-vague-response-options-produce-partisan-knowledge-gaps/)): With Carolyn E. Roush. Two survey experiments present the same small declines in unemployment and inflation under either an Obama cue or a Republican Congress cue. Respondents assess whether conditions got better, stayed about the same, or got worse. On a 0–100 evaluation scale, opposing-party rather than own-party cues change unemployment and inflation evaluations by -9.5 points (95% CI [-12.5, -6.5]) and -6.0 points (95% CI [-9.2, -2.8]) on MTurk, and by -5.2 points (95% CI [-10.6, 0.2]) and -8.6 points (95% CI [-14.2, -3.1]) on Lucid. The Lucid unemployment estimate includes zero. These are effects on evaluations of supplied information, not direct measures of factual knowledge; response-option vagueness was not randomized. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/finite-sample/know_pgap_cues).
- [Measuring Perceptions of Numerical Strength of Salient and Stereotypical Groups](https://gsood.com/research/papers/measuring_shares.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/measuring-perceptions-of-numerical-strength-of-salient-and-stereotypical-groups/)): With Doug Ahler. Misinformation and Mass Audiences. 2018. University of Texas Press. This chapter examines how to measure beliefs about the numerical size of salient and stereotypical groups. It connects systematic overestimation of stereotypical traits to broader questions about group perceptions, prejudice, and the interpretation of survey estimates. Links: [Appendix](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/2JXAYZ), [Replication Materials](https://github.com/soodoku/partisan_shares).

## Decision Making

### Group Affect
- [Inter-group Prejudice](https://gsood.com/research/papers/inter_group_prejudice.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/inter-group-prejudice/)): This note organizes explanations for inter-group prejudice, including group identity, personality, motivated beliefs, and differences in reasoning. It distinguishes possible mechanisms behind aversive beliefs and feelings rather than treating prejudice as a single process.
- [Affect, Not Ideology: A Social Identity Perspective on Polarization](https://gsood.com/research/papers/AffectNotIdeology.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/affect-not-ideology-a-social-identity-perspective-on-polarization/)): With Shanto Iyengar and Yphtach Lelkes. Public Opinion Quarterly. 76(3), 405–431, 2012. We examine polarization as social distance and hostility between partisans, rather than only disagreement over policy. Evidence from several sources shows growing dislike of opposing partisans, with policy attitudes providing an inconsistent explanation and campaign messages offering a plausible alternative. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/soodoku/partisan_affect/), [Sort of Sorted But Definitely Cold](http://gojiberries.io/sorted-or-polarized/), [The Order of Feelings](http://gojiberries.io/the-order-of-feelings/), [Affectively Polarized?](http://gojiberries.io/mass-affective-polarization/), [Party Time](https://www.gojiberries.io/party-time/), [The New York Times](https://gsood.com/research/press/NYT.POQ.pdf), [The Washington Post](https://gsood.com/research/press/WP.POQ.pdf), [Mother Jones](https://gsood.com/research/press/MJ.POQ.pdf), [Vox](https://gsood.com/research/press/AffectVox.pdf).
- [The Parties in our Heads: Misperceptions About Party Composition and Their Consequences](https://gsood.com/research/papers/partisanComposition.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/the-parties-in-our-heads-misperceptions-about-party-composition-and-their-consequences/)): With Doug Ahler. The Journal of Politics. 80(3), 964–981, 2018. Americans greatly overestimate how many party supporters belong to stereotypical groups. Survey experiments suggest that these misperceptions are not simply expressive responding or ignorance of population shares; correcting beliefs about the opposing party reduces perceived extremity and social distance. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/soodoku/partisan_heads), [FiveThirtyEight](https://gsood.com/research/press/pcomp_538.pdf), [Vox](https://gsood.com/research/press/PCompVox.pdf), [The Washington Post](https://gsood.com/research/press/PCompWP_2.pdf), [The Washington Post (2)](https://gsood.com/research/press/PCompWP_3.pdf), [Christian Science Monitor](https://gsood.com/research/press/PCompCSMonitor.pdf), [The Hill](https://gsood.com/research/press/TheHillPComp.pdf), [PBS (Twin Cities)](https://www.tptoriginals.org/how-well-do-you-know-the-other-party/), [The Partisans in our Heads](https://gsood.com/research/papers/guesswho.pdf), [Supplement to the 2015 Draft](https://gsood.com/research/papers/partisanCompositionSupplement.pdf).
- [Typecast: A Routine Mental Shortcut Causes Party Stereotyping](https://gsood.com/research/papers/typecast.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/typecast-a-routine-mental-shortcut-causes-party-stereotyping/)): With Doug Ahler. Political Behavior, 45(4), 1581–1607, 2023. We test whether the representativeness heuristic contributes to party stereotypes. Experiments involving conjunction judgments, information about group partisanship, and cognitive load suggest that this mental shortcut can distort perceptions of who belongs to each party. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/soodoku/partisan_typecast), [Appendix](https://gsood.com/research/papers/typecast_si.pdf), [Heterodox Academy](https://gsood.com/research/press/typecast_hxa.pdf).
- [All in the Eye of the Beholder: Partisan Affect and Ideological Accountability](https://gsood.com/research/papers/inNout.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/all-in-the-eye-of-the-beholder-partisan-affect-and-ideological-accountability/)): With Shanto Iyengar. In The Feeling, Thinking Citizen: Essays in Honor of Milton Lodge. 2018. Why do moderate partisans remain warm toward more extreme leaders of their own party? We find both distorted perceptions of leaders' positions and asymmetric treatment of policy disagreement: even when informed about positions, partisans do not necessarily penalize more distant co-partisan candidates. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/soodoku/partisan_accountability), [Still Close: Perceived Ideological Distance to Own and Main Opposing Party](https://gsood.com/research/papers/moving_further.pdf), [2012 Blog Post](http://gojiberries.io/moving-further-away-from-the-out-party/), [The New York Times](https://gsood.com/research/press/InOut_NYT.pdf).
- [Coming to Dislike Your Opponents: Candidate Evaluations during Presidential Campaigns](https://gsood.com/research/papers/ComingToDislike.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/coming-to-dislike-your-opponents-the-polarizing-impact-of-political-campaigns/)): With Shanto Iyengar. Candidate evaluations diverge over the 2000, 2004, and 2008 presidential campaigns, with differences across elections and measures. Ratings of both one’s own candidate and the opponent contribute. Trait-rating gaps widen faster in battleground states, while overall favorability shows a less consistent geographic pattern. These survey comparisons describe change without identifying the effects of campaigning or negative advertising. Links: [New York Times](https://gsood.com/research/press/ComingtoDislike_nyt.pdf), [Replication files (v1.0.0)](https://gsood.com/research/replication/polarcamp-v1.0.0.zip), [Code and data](https://github.com/soodoku/partisan_campaigns).
- [Partisan Vision? Partisan Bias in Simple Visual Evaluations](https://gsood.com/research/papers/partisan_vision.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/partisan-vision-partisan-bias-in-simple-visual-evaluations/)): With Carrie Roush and Alex Theodoridis. Two experiments and a survey test whether partisanship shapes simple visual evaluations. Respondents count errors in a passage, count poorly parked cars in a photograph, or count people wearing masks in a video. Pooling the writing and parking experiments yields a 0.12-standard-deviation effect (SE 0.04) favoring respondents' own party, with inference clustered by respondent. The clearest individual effect is in Democrats' parking judgments. The pooled effect persists under response caps of 10, 15, and 20, although the Lucid Republican writing contrast is sensitive to extreme responses. The strength interactions do not show consistently larger effects among strong partisans. Republicans count more masked people in the Trump-supporter video under several response caps; that comparison is descriptive and sensitive to extreme responses. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/soodoku/partisan_vision/).
- [The Hostile Audience: The Effect of Access to Broadband Internet on Partisan Affect](https://gsood.com/research/papers/BroadbandPolarization.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/the-hostile-audience-the-effect-of-access-to-broadband-internet-on-partisan-affect/)): With Yphtach Lelkes and Shanto Iyengar. American Journal of Political Science. 61(1): 5–20, 2017. We use variation in state right-of-way regulations to study the effect of broadband access on partisan hostility. Combining broadband availability with survey data from 2004 and 2008, we find greater hostility and greater consumption of partisan media where broadband access expands. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/soodoku/partisan_broadband), [The Guardian](https://gsood.com/research/press/Hostile_Guardian.pdf), [Published Version](https://gsood.com/research/papers/ajps12237_LRyl.pdf).
- [Holier Than Thou? No Large Partisan Gap in Consumption of Pornography Online](https://gsood.com/research/papers/adult.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/holier-than-thou-no-large-partisan-gap-in-consumption-of-pornography-online/)): With Lucas Shen. Journal of Quantitative Description: Digital Media, 4, 2024. Observed browsing data show that online pornography consumption is concentrated among a small share of users. Republicans consume somewhat more than Democrats in the unadjusted data, but the difference disappears after accounting for age and gender. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/themains/adult).
- [Which Pakistanis Hold Militant Groups in “Low Regard”? Three Interviewers in Blair et al.’s Endorsement Experiment](https://gsood.com/research/papers/endorsement.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/do-pakistanis-hold-militant-groups-in-low-regard/)): Three of the 75 interviewers in a Pakistan survey recorded the same four policy answers in most of their interviews. Their 313 respondents came almost entirely from middle- and high-income households. Excluding their interviews reduces the estimated difference between poor and middle-class respondents from 2.2 to 1.0 points on a 100-point scale. The remaining data are consistent with both zero and the published estimate. The average penalty for a militant group’s endorsement grows from 1.3 to 2.1 points, but that average says little about how many people favored the endorsement. Links: [Code and Data](https://github.com/finite-sample/endorsement).
- [The Impact of Social Desirability Pressures on Whites’ Endorsement of Racial Stereotypes: A Comparison Between Oral and ACASI Reports in a National Survey](https://gsood.com/research/papers/StereotypesAboutSD.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/hidden-racial-prejudice-impact-of-social-desirability-pressures-on-endorsement-of-racial-stereotypes/)): With Jon Krosnick, Tobias Stark, and Floor van Maaren. Sociological Methods & Research, 51(2), 605–631, 2022. We compare White respondents' racial stereotype reports in confidential computer-assisted and oral interviews in the 2008 American National Election Study. Confidential responses are slightly more negative about both Black and White people and have no greater predictive validity, casting doubt on a large social-desirability distortion in the oral measures. Links: [Replication Materials](https://osf.io/jdv7r/), [Online Supplement](https://gsood.com/research/papers/StereotypesAboutSDAppendix.pdf).
- [Principled Partisan Affect? Evidence from Two Survey Experiments](https://gsood.com/research/papers/principled.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/principled-partisan-affect-evidence-from-two-survey-experiments/)): With Douglas J. Ahler and Carolyn E. Roush. Is partisan affect principled? In a 2013 MTurk experiment, reports of declining rather than sustained support for a leader after controversy lowered estimated warmth toward fellow partisans, suggesting a possible preference for loyalty. In a 2018 YouGov experiment, portraying opponents as fair-minded modestly improved estimated trait ratings, with little estimated movement in warmth. Portraying allies as biased produced no clear penalty, but many readers also reported that their party was about as biased as expected. The evidence is suggestive: uncertain estimates, missing warmth ratings, bundled article features, and incomplete comparisons prevent firm conclusions about effect sizes, mechanisms, or a partisan double standard. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/soodoku/partisan_principled).
- [Pareto Partisan? Relative Gains and Support for Public Policy](https://gsood.com/research/papers/pareto_partisan.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/pareto-partisan-relative-gains-and-support-for-public-policy/)): With Alexander G. Theodoridis. If people prefer more for both sides to less for both, everyone should select the plan giving both sides more. In a 2018 CCES highway choice, only 35.0% of Democrats and 27.1% of Republicans did so; the rest chose smaller allocations that left their side ahead. In a post-election experiment, raising opponents’ income gain from 3% to 7%, while keeping the own-party gain at 5%, changed policy support by -20.0 points on a 0–100 scale (95% CI [-23.9, -16.1]). Relative partisan gains affect support, but the exercises do not distinguish spite from dislike of falling behind; the highway comparison also changes total spending. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/soodoku/partisan_pareto).

### Deliberation
- [What Would Dahl Say? An Appraisal of the Democratic Credentials of the Deliberative Polls and Other Mini-publics](https://gsood.com/research/papers/DahlSays.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/what-would-dahl-say-an-appraisal-of-the-democratic-credentials-of-the-deliberative-polls-and-other-mini-publics/)): With Ian O'Flynn. Deliberative Mini-Publics. 41–58, 2014. ECPR Press. We assess deliberative polls and other mini-publics using Robert Dahl's criteria for a democratic process: inclusion, effective participation, enlightened understanding, voting equality, and control of the agenda. The chapter examines where these institutions meet the criteria and where their democratic claims require qualification.
- [How Can You Think That? Deliberation and the Learning of Opposing Arguments](https://gsood.com/research/papers/LearningOfArguments.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/how-can-you-think-that-deliberation-and-the-learning-of-opposing-arguments/)): With Robert C. Luskin and James S. Fishkin. Using open-ended responses from a Deliberative Poll on schooling in Northern Ireland, we compare the reasons articulated by returning participants and contemporaneous controls. Participants gave somewhat more reasons, but the estimate is imprecise and participation was self-selected. The samples differed little in directional balance. Among returnees, repertoires moved toward balance chiefly because supporting reasons declined, and the estimate is sensitive to coder choice. Links: [Replication Materials](https://github.com/soodoku/dp_nireland).
- [Deliberation and Learning: Evidence From Deliberative Polls](https://gsood.com/research/papers/deliberation_learning.pdf) ([page](https://gsood.com/research/deliberation-and-learning-evidence-from-deliberative-polls/)): With Robert C. Luskin and James S. Fishkin. Across 27 Deliberative Polls, factual knowledge increased by an average of 14.3 percentage points, a relative gain of 39.3%. In two polls with control groups, attendees gained an average of 11.2 percentage points more than controls. Measurements before arrival, on arrival, and after deliberation in two studies show substantial gains before participants arrive. The gender gap narrows but remains. Across 20 polls with poll-specific education cutoffs, the gap between more and less educated attendees widens.
